drop.title: The One Knob That Tames Newton's Method

title: The One Knob That Tames
Newton's Method
slides.dek: Newton's method takes the whole tangent step, every time. Scale that step by a single factor and you hold a dial that makes the same fractal fast, safe, or suicidal.

slides.body: Newton's method finds a zero by sliding down the tangent line, from a guess to where that line crosses the axis, then starting again. That slide has a fixed length, p over p'. Write a single relaxation factor *h* in front of it, take *h* times the usual step, and one number becomes a dial: h = 1 is ordinary Newton, below 1 is a *damped* (timid) step, above 1 is an *over-relaxed* (greedy) one. Three completely different personalities for the same method, set by one knob.

Sweep h across thousands of starting guesses and two facts fall out. On the well-behaved z³-1 the average steps to a root is a clean valley bottoming *exactly at h = 1* (about 4.9), with a cliff to no convergence near h = 2. On the cautionary z³-2z+2 one setting alone traps guesses forever, again *h = 1*, where 1.1% of the plane drops into an endless 0, 1, 0, 1 cycle. Near a root each step shrinks the error by |1-h|, zero only at h = 1, which is exactly where Newton's digit-doubling lives. The fastest setting is the one with no margin.

lines.sub: keep the numerical-analysis vein warm after #053's newton fractal, but rotate research to app: one live dial instead of a static four-map gallery. the whole change is a single factor h on the step, z - h*p/p'

three modules over one knob: two live basin maps under a single slider (z^3-1 easy, z^3-2z+2 with a trap), two sweep curves with a live marker, and the mechanism as an error ladder plus a tradeoff table

checked offline first, 18/18: roots stay fixed for every h, the near-root error ratio equals |1-h|, mean steps on z^3-1 bottom at h=1 (4.85) and wall off past h~1.95, and z^3-2z+2 traps 1.12% at h=1, healed by any detuning

slides.big:
the fastest step
is the only one
*with no margin.*
slides.sub: Turn one dial from 0.1 to 2.0 and watch two Newton fractals answer at once. Damp it and both go pale and slow; push past h = 1.9 and the whole plane detonates to black. See why h = 1 is the measured optimum on an easy polynomial and the single fragile setting on a hard one, where 1.1% of the plane falls into a 0, 1, 0, 1 trap that any small detuning heals. The safeguard hiding in every real solver is just this: stop always taking the whole step.
